questions.prompt: A link in a Super Bowl advert gets **200,000 clicks/s** for ten minutes. It lives on one Redis shard that handles about 100k ops/s. Analytics for the advertiser matter. What is the best mitigation?

options.text: Re-shard Redis with more nodes so the key gets more capacity.
options.explanation: Wrong. Consistent hashing still places one key on one shard, so adding nodes doesn't spread a single hot key.

options.text: Return a 301 with no cache headers so browsers stop coming back.
options.explanation: Wrong for this case. Each viewer clicks once, so browser caching saves little, and you'd lose control of the link. Most of the 200k/s are different people.

options.text: Serve from edge or application-local copies with an explicit freshness policy, and capture click events using the required delivery guarantee.
options.explanation: Correct. Replicating read-serving copies relieves the single hot partition. Analytics preservation depends on durable capture and duplicate handling, not batching alone.

options.text: Rate limit the link to 100k clicks/s.
options.explanation: Wrong. Dropping half the advertiser's traffic during their most expensive minute is the worst possible outcome.

questions.workedExample: A single hot key remains on one partition when you merely add shards. Replicate its read-serving copies across application servers or edge locations, and measure whether that distribution handles the observed skew. A short TTL bounds cache age only under the stated refresh and upstream-freshness rules; abuse blocking may need an independent check. Batched analytics need durable buffering, retries and deduplication if loss is unacceptable.

lessons.title: Expand the namespace and preserve regional uniqueness
lessons.summary: Seven characters cannot hold ten years at a billion new links a day.
lessons.body:
Now increase the assumed workload tenfold: one billion new links a day and 300,000 redirects a second. Earlier units established cache freshness and non-reused ID ranges; apply both when expanding the namespace and serving regions.

## At 10x scale

At 1 billion new links a day and 300k redirects/s:

- **Seven characters is no longer enough** for 10 years (3.65 trillion links vs 3.5 trillion codes). Move to 8 characters (218 trillion) for new links. An 8-character string can never equal a 7-character one, so new generated links use exactly eight characters (left-pad short encodings), with a fresh permutation over all 218 trillion 8-character values. Also revise alias reservations or atomically skip already-claimed aliases.
- **Storage reaches petabytes** (about 1.8 PB raw over 10 years). Move cold links to cheaper storage if latency permits; expire them only when the retention contract allows it.
- **Go multi-region.** Replicate mapping rows asynchronously to serve redirects locally, with a separate freshness policy for deletion and blocking. Durable disjoint ID ranges avoid cross-region coordination on each generated-code create while unused ranges remain. A fresh mapping can be missing elsewhere until replication catches up; a reachable home-region fallback can resolve that miss.
- **Push redirects to the edge.** CDN workers (Cloudflare Workers, Lambda@Edge) can hold hot mappings and reduce origin work; end-to-end latency still needs measurement, shipping click logs back in batches.
- **Shard the analytics pipeline** by code and pre-aggregate at the edge before sending upstream.

The revised forecast needs about 3.65 trillion codes, exceeding the roughly 3.52 trillion seven-character space. The storage budget also grows, but it remains a separate constraint from identifier capacity.

## Distinguish generated codes from aliases

A region can create generated links during a bounded network partition while it still owns unused, durable ranges. It must stop or reject creation when its range is exhausted; disconnected regions cannot safely allocate the same new range. Custom aliases are different because a user can request the same text in two regions. Route that uniqueness decision to a home authority, or reject and defer alias creation while the authority is unreachable.

Asynchronous replicas support local redirect reads with a documented freshness delay. A fallback to the home region improves a fresh-link miss only when that region is reachable. Abuse blocking and deletions need a separate propagation or authoritative check policy; immutable destinations do not make these changes instantly consistent.

## Key takeaways

- Seven characters cannot hold ten years at a billion new links a day.
- Use an exact new code length and revisit alias reservations.
- Disjoint preallocated ranges support partitioned creation; custom aliases still need global uniqueness.

## Further reading

- [DynamoDB: conditional writes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Expressions.ConditionExpressions.html)
- [Python: numeric operations and divmod](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#divmod)

questions.prompt: An updated forecast requires more distinct codes than the seven-character namespace contains. Existing links must keep working. Which migration fits?

options.text: Reissue old codes for new destinations.
options.explanation: That breaks saved links and can send users to the wrong destination.

options.text: Rely on faster base62 encoding to increase the namespace.
options.explanation: Compute speed does not change the number of representable strings.

options.text: Add cache shards while keeping the same exhausted code space.
options.explanation: Cache capacity does not create new identifier values.

options.text: Issue new generated codes at a fixed longer length, preserve old mappings and resolve possible custom-alias conflicts.
options.explanation: Correct. Distinct fixed lengths separate generated namespaces, but existing aliases still need conditional collision handling or revised reservations.

questions.workedExample: The capacity forecast is already supplied; the task is to evolve safely. Keep the old resolver and mappings, introduce an exact new generated length including padding, and preserve uniqueness within it. Check custom aliases and abandoned ranges before rollout.

questions.prompt: You expand to three regions so redirects are served locally. Generated-code link creation must remain available during a bounded partition while preallocated ID ranges remain; globally unique custom aliases are out of scope. Which choices fit? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give each region its own pre-allocated ID ranges, so regions generate codes without talking to each other.
options.explanation: Correct. Disjoint ranges guarantee uniqueness with no cross-region coordination, so a partitioned region can still create links.

options.text: Replicate the links table asynchronously to all regions.
options.explanation: Correct for independently allocated mapping rows. Deletions, expiry and abuse blocking still need a freshness and propagation policy.

options.text: On a local miss, check the link's home region before returning 404.
options.explanation: Correct. It covers replication lag only when the home region is reachable; it cannot resolve an unknown link during that region's isolation. The home region can be encoded in the ID range, so you know where to ask.

options.text: Use a single global counter with synchronous cross-region consensus for every create.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Every create would depend on cross-region coordination, preventing isolated regions from creating links under the stated requirement.

options.text: Use 301 with an infinite cache so other regions are rarely asked.
options.explanation: Incorrect. It doesn't help create availability, and it gives up analytics and the ability to disable abusive links.

questions.workedExample: Durably allocate disjoint ranges before a partition, never reuse ranges and stop when a region exhausts its allocation. Replicate mappings asynchronously and use a reachable home region for fresh misses. Generated-code availability does not extend to globally contested custom aliases, and immutable destinations do not remove deletion or blocking consistency requirements.

lessons.title: Set limiter guarantees and estimate capacity
lessons.summary: Separate policy targets from measured Redis capacity.
lessons.body:
A rate limiter caps how many requests a client can make in a period. It protects services from abuse and runaway clients, enforces pricing tiers ("free plan: 100 requests per minute"), and stops one tenant from starving everyone else.

On one server it's an in-memory counter. The interview is about making it work across hundreds of API servers, at a million requests a second, adding no more than a millisecond, and staying correct when clients race each other.

## Step 1: Requirements

**Functional**

- Limit requests per **key** (API key, user ID, IP address, or a combination) according to **rules** such as "100 requests/minute per API key on `POST /charges`".
- Support several rules per request (per-second burst limit *and* per-day quota).
- When a limit is exceeded, reject with **HTTP 429 Too Many Requests** and tell the client when to retry.
- Rules can be changed without redeploying.

**Non-functional**

- **Low overhead**: the check sits on every request, so it must add under ~1–2 ms at p99.
- **Highly available**: if the limiter is down, the API should keep working.
- **Approximately accurate**: a small overshoot (a few percent) is fine; massively over-admitting is not.
- **Distributed**: limits are global across all API servers, not per server.

## Step 2: Estimates

Assume an API fleet handling **1 million requests/s** at peak, with **10 million active keys** a day.

Every request needs one limiter check, which is one Redis call (a single Lua script). The number of Redis shards follows from dividing the check rate by what one shard handles:

The check rate sets throughput demand. Benchmark the actual script at the required tail latency, then allow for uneven keys, replication and failover rather than running every shard at its maximum.

Count the state retained by the limiter:

Memory depends on concurrently retained keys, rules per key and the actual stored representation. Daily unique clients are not automatically the number of counters resident at once.

These are illustrative workload inputs, not measured Redis capacity or memory bounds. Actual key strings, objects, allocator overhead, scripts, replication and network tails must be measured. A single atomic call reduces both race windows and network hops.

> [!note] Content gap: deployment benchmarks
> No reproducible deployment benchmark is supplied for the stated 1–2 ms target or per-shard throughput/footprint. Universal capacity and latency estimates are omitted; the workload and target above use explicit assumptions.

## Key takeaways

- Separate policy targets from measured Redis capacity.
- Count checks, active keys and rules independently.
- Choose the consequence of counter resets before selecting storage.

## Further reading

- [Stripe: rate and concurrency limiting](https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters)
- [Redis: benchmark limitations](https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/management/optimization/benchmarks/)

questions.prompt: A Redis limiter benchmark passes at the required tail latency, but the proposed deployment would keep every primary at that measured maximum during peak traffic. What should change?

options.text: Nothing: a successful benchmark guarantees the same latency during failover.
options.explanation: The benchmark does not prove capacity after a node loss, skew or a deployment.

options.text: Choose a fixed hundred-shard deployment for every workload.
options.explanation: A universal fleet size ignores workload, script cost and operating targets.

options.text: Remove the limit so requests never reach Redis.
options.explanation: That removes the protection requirement instead of meeting it.

options.text: Reserve measured operating margin and test skew, failure redistribution and the actual script.
options.explanation: Correct. Headroom must cover the scenarios the service promises to survive, rather than merely the average allocation.

questions.workedExample: Determine what one shard can sustain at the target latency, then test the distribution of real keys and the failure scenarios. Count memory and replication separately. A generic operations-per-second figure does not establish the capacity of this script.

lessons.title: Choose identity, rule storage and shard routing
lessons.summary: Put checks before backend work and return useful retry guidance.
lessons.body:
## Step 3: API

The limiter is usually an internal service called by the API gateway, or a library or sidecar inside it. Lyft's open-source Envoy rate limit service is a gRPC service with essentially this shape:

```
ShouldRateLimit(domain, descriptors[])
  -> {overall: OK | OVER_LIMIT,
      statuses: [{limit, remaining,
                  resetSeconds}]}
```

To the *external* client, a rejected request looks like:

```
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 12
RateLimit-Limit: 100
RateLimit-Remaining: 0
RateLimit-Reset: 12
```

429 is defined in RFC 6585, and `Retry-After` is a standard HTTP header (RFC 9110). The `RateLimit-*` headers above are illustrative, non-standard field names from an earlier draft. The IETF HTTPAPI draft evolves structured quota fields; check the current draft rather than treating these names as a final standard. APIs can also define their own quota-header contracts; a field name alone does not establish units or reset semantics. Whatever the names, good headers matter: well-behaved clients back off instead of hammering you.

> [!warning] Retry storms
> If every rejected client retries exactly at the `Retry-After` time, they all come back in the same instant. Client SDKs should add random jitter to retries, and the server can vary `Retry-After` slightly per client.

## Step 4: Data model

Two kinds of data:

**Rules** are small, read constantly, changed rarely. Store them in a database or config repo and push them to every limiter instance, which caches them in memory.

Illustrative YAML configuration for this design, rather than an Envoy configuration format:

```yaml
# Identity and route choose the quota key.
domain: payments
key: api_key
path: /charges
# Capacity permits a burst of 100 requests.
capacity: 100
# Average allowance is 100 per 60 seconds.
refill_tokens: 100
refill_seconds: 60
algorithm: token_bucket
```

**Counters** are tiny, extremely hot and short-lived. Keep them in Redis (or Memcached), keyed by rule and client:

An illustrative Redis hash contains the balance and last refill time. These commands require a Redis connection; the timestamp is a fixture, not the current time.

```console
HSET rl:payments:/charges:{key_abc123} \
  tokens 37 last_refill 1727780000.123
HGETALL rl:payments:/charges:{key_abc123}
```

The hash contains 37 tokens and the supplied refill timestamp. Read, refill and decrement still need an atomic script; these two commands only demonstrate the stored representation.

The braces are a Redis Cluster **hash tag**: only the part inside `{}` is hashed to pick the shard. Tagging the *client* key puts all of one client's counters (burst limit, daily quota) on the same shard, so one Lua script can check several rules atomically, while different clients still spread across shards. Tagging the rule name instead (`{payments:/charges}`) would be a classic mistake: every client of that endpoint would land on one shard.

For this availability-first example, decide explicitly whether resetting counters is acceptable. A reset can grant a full new burst to every affected key, not merely a few percent overshoot. Security controls and billable quotas may require durable accounting or a different failure policy.

### Choosing the key

What you limit by matters as much as the algorithm:

- **API key or user ID** for authenticated traffic: precise and fair.
- **IP address** for anonymous traffic, with care. Thousands of mobile users can share one carrier-grade NAT address, and an IPv6 attacker can rotate through billions of addresses in a /64. Choose a prefix grouping from actual allocation patterns rather than treating /64 as a universal customer identity, and account for shared IPv4 addresses.
- **Combinations** for specific abuse: per (account, IP) limits on login can reduce some abuse, but distributed credential stuffing needs additional account/global signals and monitoring.

For anonymous signup protection, layer network limits with independently useful identity signals or challenges; a freely resettable session token is weak evidence. Trust forwarded client addresses only through a configured trusted proxy chain, never an arbitrary internet-supplied header. For a security-sensitive route, choose a bounded local fallback or fail closed when the shared limiter is unavailable.

## Step 5: High-level design

```
 Client
   |
   v
 API gateway  <---- rules (cached,
   |   |              pushed on change)
   |   | check
   |   v
   | Limiter (lib/sidecar/svc)
   |   |
   |   v
   | Redis cluster
   | (counters, sharded by key)
   v
 Backend services
```

**Where to put it?**

- **In the client**: never trust it; clients can be modified.
- **In each service**: duplicated logic, inconsistent rules.
- **In the API gateway or a sidecar** (Envoy, Kong, AWS API Gateway): one place, before traffic reaches backends. This is the usual answer.
- **As a separate service** the gateway calls: centralises logic, costs an extra hop. Envoy's model is a sidecar that calls a central rate limit service backed by Redis.

## Key takeaways

- Put checks before backend work and return useful retry guidance.
- Hash-tag the client identity to co-locate its rules without one endpoint-wide hot shard.
- Consider NAT sharing, IPv6 rotation and retry jitter when choosing policy.

## Further reading

- [Envoy: global rate limiting](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/other_features/global_rate_limiting)
- [Redis: cluster hash tags](https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/reference/cluster-spec/)
- [RFC 6585: HTTP 429](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585)

questions.prompt: Your limiter runs on a 20-shard Redis Cluster. Counter keys look like `rl:{search}:user_123`. Dashboards show one shard at 100% CPU and the other 19 nearly idle, and most traffic is to `/search`. What's wrong?

options.text: Redis Cluster hashes the whole key, so `user_123` must be a hot user.
options.explanation: Wrong. When a key contains `{...}`, Redis Cluster hashes only the part inside the braces. One hot user wouldn't explain *all* search traffic landing on one shard.

options.text: The hash tag `{search}` sends every client's `/search` counter to the same slot. Tag the client instead, e.g. `rl:search:{user_123}`.
options.explanation: Correct. Only the tagged part picks the shard, so every key with `{search}` maps to one slot. Tagging the client spreads clients across shards and still co-locates one client's rules for multi-rule Lua scripts.

options.text: 20 shards is too few; add more.
options.explanation: Wrong. Adding shards can't help: all `{search}` keys map to the same hash slot, which lives on one shard however many you have.

options.text: Lua scripts are single-threaded, so one shard always does all the scripting.
options.explanation: Wrong. Each shard runs its own scripts on its own keys. The imbalance comes from key placement, not from Lua.

questions.workedExample: Redis Cluster uses a valid hash tag inside braces when selecting a slot. Every key tagged with search therefore selects the same slot, regardless of the user suffix. Tagging the client instead keeps that client’s rules together while allowing different clients to occupy different slots. Distinct tags may still collide, so verify actual distribution; adding shards does not split a single hot slot.

questions.prompt: You must rate limit an **unauthenticated** signup endpoint against bots, served to both IPv4 and IPv6 clients. Which practices are sound? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use an IPv6 prefix limit, with prefix size chosen from deployment evidence, to reduce easy rotation within an allocated block.
options.explanation: Correct. A /64 is a possible grouping, not a universal customer identity. Allocation sizes and sharing vary.

options.text: Set IPv4 limits loosely enough that many users behind one carrier-grade NAT address aren't blocked.
options.explanation: Correct. Mobile carriers and offices put thousands of users behind one public IPv4 address. A tight per-IP limit there blocks real users.

options.text: Layer network limits with harder-to-obtain identity signals or challenges; assess whether a device/session token is cheaply resettable.
options.explanation: Correct. A freely minted session token provides little protection. Evaluate acquisition cost, privacy, false positives and bypasses.

options.text: Trust a client-supplied `X-Forwarded-For` header from the internet as the client's IP.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Anyone can set that header. Only trust it when your own load balancer or CDN adds it, and read the address that your own infrastructure appended.

options.text: Fail open on this endpoint if the limiter is down, because availability always wins.
options.explanation: Incorrect for this case. Signup abuse protection is security-sensitive, like login. Failing closed (or falling back to a strict local limit) is the safer choice here.

questions.workedExample: IPv6 addresses can rotate within a block; IPv4 addresses can be shared by many legitimate users. Choose network grouping and thresholds from actual allocation patterns, then add independently useful identity or challenge signals. Trust forwarded addresses only through a correctly configured trusted proxy chain.

questions.prompt: A partner's batch job gets rate limited, and your server returns `Retry-After: 30` to each of its 5,000 worker threads. Exactly 30 seconds later, all 5,000 retry within the same 100 ms and are rejected again, over and over. What best fixes this?

options.text: Return `Retry-After: 0` so they retry immediately and spread out naturally.
options.explanation: Wrong. Immediate retries just turn the batch into a tight loop that hammers the limiter continuously.

options.text: Switch from 429 to 503 so clients treat it as an outage.
options.explanation: Wrong. 503 signals server unavailability rather than a client exceeding its quota, and many clients retry 503s more aggressively.

options.text: Add jitter: clients retry after `Retry-After` plus a random delay (and back off exponentially on repeated 429s), and the server can vary `Retry-After` slightly per request.
options.explanation: Correct. Independent random waits reduce synchronisation in expectation while respecting the provider minimum delay. They do not guarantee smooth arrivals, recovery or admission; retain retry and deadline budgets.

options.text: Raise the partner's limit to 5,000 per burst.
options.explanation: Wrong as the fix. It might help this partner today, but the herd behaviour remains and returns at the next limit. Fix the retry pattern.

questions.workedExample: A shared retry deadline synchronises workers. Respect the server’s minimum delay, then independently randomise an additional wait within the remaining deadline. On repeated retryable failures, increase the backoff ceiling and cap attempts. Random choices reduce synchronisation in expectation; they do not guarantee smooth arrivals or that the next requests will be admitted.

lessons.title: Compare fixed windows with rolling-count estimates
lessons.summary: Fixed windows allow a double burst across an aligned boundary.
lessons.body:
A limiter rule might allow 100 requests per minute. The question is which minute: an aligned calendar interval or every possible rolling interval. This unit compares the counting algorithms before the next unit introduces a burst-and-average contract.

## Deep dive 1: Algorithms

### Fixed window counter

Count requests in each calendar window (`12:00:00–12:00:59`); reject once the count passes the limit. One `INCR` plus an `EXPIRE`.

- **Pro**: trivial, one integer per key.
- **Con: boundary bursts.** With a 100/min limit, a client can send 100 at 12:00:59 and 100 more at 12:01:00, so 200 requests in two seconds.

### Sliding request timestamp log

Store a timestamp for every request (a Redis sorted set). On each request, drop entries older than the window and count what's left.

- **Pro**: exact for the chosen rolling request-count interval when pruning, counting and recording accepted requests happen atomically.
- **Con: memory.** A limit of 10,000/hour stores up to 10,000 timestamps per key. At 10 million keys, that's prohibitive.

### Sliding window counter

Keep fixed-window counts for the current and previous window. A true rolling window ending now still overlaps the tail end of the previous window, so count the previous window in proportion to that overlap:

```formula reference
E = P(1 − t / w) + C
where
E: estimated requests in the trailing window
P: requests counted in the previous aligned window
C: requests counted so far in the current aligned window
t: elapsed time in the current window, in seconds, from zero up to but excluding w
w: window duration in seconds
In words: count all current-window requests and estimate the still-overlapping part of the previous window; this assumes the previous requests were spread evenly.
```

Halfway through a window, the estimate keeps half the previous count and all of the current count. If earlier requests were concentrated near the boundary, that proportional estimate can be wrong.

- **Pro**: two integers per key, smooths boundary bursts.
- **Con**: approximate; it assumes requests in the previous window were evenly spread. Cloudflare reported around 0.003% incorrect decisions in its published workload. That historical empirical result is not a worst-case error bound; concentrated traffic can produce large errors.

## Key takeaways

- Fixed windows allow a double burst across an aligned boundary.
- Timestamp logs give exact counting semantics when implemented atomically.
- Two-window counters approximate a rolling interval and can err under concentrated traffic.

## Further reading

- [Cloudflare: measured sliding-counter approximation](https://blog.cloudflare.com/counting-things-a-lot-of-different-things/)
- [Redis: atomic increment and rate-limit patterns](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/incr/)

questions.prompt: A client sends a full allowance just before an aligned minute ends, then another full allowance immediately after it begins. Why can a fixed-window limiter accept both?

options.text: It enforces every rolling minute exactly.
options.explanation: Exact rolling enforcement would count the earlier burst while it remains in the trailing interval.

options.text: It spreads requests evenly across the minute.
options.explanation: Fixed-window counting does not pace arrivals.

options.text: It has no limit at all.
options.explanation: Each aligned window still has its own cap.

options.text: Each burst belongs to a different counter window.
options.explanation: Correct. Resetting at the aligned boundary permits two allowances close together without exceeding either individual window.

questions.workedExample: Place the two bursts on opposite sides of the reset. Each counter stays within its own cap, but a short interval crossing the boundary contains both. Choose an exact rolling log or an explicitly approximate scheme when that boundary behaviour is unacceptable.

questions.prompt: A two-window counter weights the previous window by how much still overlaps the trailing interval. What makes its decision approximate?

options.text: It knows the previous total but not when those requests occurred inside that window.
options.explanation: Correct. Proportional weighting assumes an even distribution that bursts may violate.

options.text: It cannot count any requests in the current window.
options.explanation: The current count is retained in full; uncertainty concerns the older window’s distribution.

options.text: It ignores the previous window entirely.
options.explanation: That would describe a fixed-window decision, not the weighted approximation.

options.text: Redis cannot increment counters atomically.
options.explanation: Atomic increments are supported; atomicity does not recover discarded timestamps.

questions.workedExample: Imagine all previous-window requests arrived near its end. A proportional estimate may discard some even though they are all still inside the rolling interval. A timestamp log retains that timing detail but needs more memory and atomic pruning/counting/admission.

lessons.title: Implement burst limits with atomic refill checks
lessons.summary: Bucket capacity sets burst size; refill rate sets the long-run allowance.
lessons.body:
### Token bucket

Each key has a bucket that holds up to a fixed number of tokens and is topped up at a steady rate. Each request takes a token; an empty bucket means reject. Instead of a timer adding tokens, store just `tokens` and `last_refill` and work out the refill lazily on each request:

```formula reference
T_new = min(B, T + Δt r)
where
T_new: token balance after refill and before this request spends a token
T: previous token balance
B: maximum token balance, defining the available burst capacity
Δt: nonnegative elapsed time since the last accounted refill, in seconds
r: refill rate in tokens per second
min: choose the smaller value, preventing accumulated tokens from exceeding capacity
In words: idle time earns tokens at the refill rate, but the bucket never holds more than its burst capacity.
```

For example, five idle seconds at one token per second add five tokens if space remains. A long idle period only fills the bucket to capacity; it does not build an unlimited allowance.

The formula assumes the current time has not moved backwards. The Python fixture clamps negative elapsed time to zero; production timestamp persistence must also avoid granting the same elapsed interval twice after a clock regression.

```python
def refill(tokens, elapsed, cap, rate):
    # Clamp time if the clock regresses.
    earned = max(0, elapsed) * rate
    # Cap bursts after long idle time.
    return min(cap, tokens + earned)

print(refill(2, 5, 10, 1))
print(refill(2, 60, 10, 1))
# 7 then 10: refill stops at capacity.
```

This fixture checks refill arithmetic, not distributed admission. Production code must atomically update the token balance and timestamp and define how clock changes and failover are handled.

- **Pro**: separates maximum stored burst allowance from the long-run refill rate. Two numbers per key. Stripe’s published implementation describes this algorithm.
- **Con**: two parameters to tune; bursts are allowed by design, which might not suit a fragile downstream.

### Leaky bucket

Requests enter a FIFO queue drained at a fixed rate. An ideal fixed-rate drain paces output, which suits traffic shaping in front of something fragile, but queued requests wait, and bursts are delayed rather than served. A meter that rejects excess traffic and a queue that delays it have different client-visible behaviour; define which meaning is intended.

> [!tip] Default answer
> Token bucket for explicit burst-plus-average limits; sliding counters approximate rolling windows but do not provide exact rolling-window enforcement.

## Deep dive 2: Correctness under concurrency

Hundreds of gateway nodes check the same key at the same moment. A naive "read count, compare, write count + 1" is a race: two servers both read 99, both allow, both write 100, and the client got 101.

Fixes:

- **Atomic primitives.** For fixed windows, `INCR` is atomic and returns the new value: `INCR key`, then `EXPIRE key 60` on first creation, and compare the returned value with the limit. If the process dies between the two commands the key never expires, so do both in a Lua script or an appropriate transaction. Repeatedly extending a relative TTL changes expiration semantics unless the key includes the fixed window or the expiry is an absolute window boundary.
- **Lua scripts.** For token buckets, run the read-refill-decrement-write as a single Redis Lua script. Redis executes a script atomically on its node, preventing interleaved updates there in one round trip. Atomic execution is not a durability guarantee: Redis Cluster's asynchronous replication can lose acknowledged state on failover, granting extra allowance unless the wider policy accounts for it.
- **Use the server's clock.** If every gateway passes its own `now`, clock skew between gateways distorts refills. Read time inside the script (`redis.call('TIME')`) so one clock is authoritative per key.

Redis Cluster maps keys to hash slots. The client-tag design co-locates that client's rules for one script; a global fleet counter or IP/account combination can require other slots, so arbitrary combined rules are not automatically atomic.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: A small jar of admission tickets
> Tickets are replenished steadily, but the jar has a fixed capacity. A visitor can spend several saved tickets together.
>
> **How it maps:** Stored tickets are burst allowance; replenishment is the sustained rate; rejecting an empty jar prevents spending future allowance.
>
> **Where it stops:** Distributed servers must atomically share the balance and account for time and failover; separate jars do not automatically enforce a global limit.

## Key takeaways

- Bucket capacity sets burst size; refill rate sets the long-run allowance.
- Perform read, refill, decrement and persistence in one atomic operation.
- Keep fixed-window expiry and clock semantics explicit.

## Further reading

- [Redis: atomic increment and rate-limit patterns](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/incr/)
- [Stripe: rate and concurrency limiting](https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters)
- [Redis: scripting atomicity](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/programmability/eval-intro/)

questions.prompt: Your API serves a mobile app that, on launch, fires **15 requests in under a second**, then is quiet. You want an average of **1 request/second** per user. Which algorithm fits best?

options.text: Fixed window of 1 request per 1-second window.
options.explanation: Wrong. It accepts at most one per fixed window (possibly two if the burst straddles a boundary), far short of the requested launch burst.

options.text: Leaky bucket draining 1 request/s.
options.explanation: Wrong. A leaky bucket smooths output to exactly 1/s, so the 15 launch requests would queue for up to 15 seconds, making the app feel broken.

options.text: Token bucket with capacity 20 and refill rate 1 token/s.
options.explanation: Correct. The bucket starts full, so the 15-request launch burst is served immediately, while the 1 token/s refill enforces the long-run average. This is exactly the burst-plus-average shape token buckets are designed for.

options.text: Sliding window log with a limit of 1 per second.
options.explanation: Wrong. It is exact, but exact enforcement of 1/s rejects the burst just as the fixed window does, and it costs more memory.

questions.workedExample: The launch needs several requests immediately, so the bucket must already hold enough tokens for that burst. The refill rate controls how quickly that allowance returns after use. A long idle period cannot accumulate more than the capacity. A strict one-request rolling interval instead rejects most of the launch burst; queue-based shaping delays it.

questions.prompt: Each of 200 gateway nodes implements the limit as: read the Redis count; if it is below the limit, separately write back one more and allow. Under load, clients exceed their limits. Why, and what's the fix?

options.text: Redis is losing writes; enable AOF persistence.
options.explanation: Wrong. Persistence affects durability across restarts, not concurrent correctness. The writes aren't lost; they overwrite each other.

options.text: Read-modify-write race: two nodes read the same value and both allow. Use an atomic operation (`INCR` and compare the returned value, or a Lua script).
options.explanation: Correct. Between GET and SET another node can read the same count. Redis executes `INCR` and Lua scripts atomically, so each request sees a unique, up-to-date count in one round trip.

options.text: The limit is too high; halve it to compensate.
options.explanation: Wrong. Halving the limit hides the bug inconsistently: overshoot depends on concurrency, so quiet clients are now over-restricted while busy ones still overshoot.

options.text: Use a distributed lock (e.g. Redlock) around each check.
options.explanation: A correctly enforced lock can serialize the check, but distributed leases require careful failure handling and add coordination. Atomic operations at the store directly serialize this single-key update.

questions.workedExample:
Interleave two gateways, A and B, with limit 100 and count 99:

```
A: GET -> 99   (99 < 100, allow)
B: GET -> 99   (99 < 100, allow)
A: SET 100
B: SET 100
```

Two requests allowed, count says 100: the client got 101. Fix:

A native Redis Lua script can combine the increment, first-key expiry and decision. The caller supplies an aligned-minute key as KEYS[1] and a limit such as 100 as ARGV[1].

```lua
-- KEYS[1] includes the aligned minute.
-- INCR returns the updated count.
local n = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1])
if n == 1 then
  -- Expiry cleans up an old minute key.
  redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], 60)
end
local limit = tonumber(ARGV[1])
-- 1 allows; 0 rejects beyond the limit.
return n <= limit and 1 or 0
```

In a local Redis fixture with the count set to 99, successive calls return 1 then 0: request 100 is allowed and request 101 is rejected. This counts attempted requests, including rejections. The key’s minute identifier, rather than its cleanup TTL, defines the fixed window.

(Run the INCR and EXPIRE together in a Lua script; a plain MULTI cannot branch on the queued INCR result so a crash between them can't leave a key that never expires.)

For a token bucket, put refill + decrement in one Lua script so the whole step is atomic, and read time with `redis.call('TIME')` to avoid gateway clock skew.

lessons.title: Bound fallback, leases and regional quota shares
lessons.summary: Choose fail-open or fail-closed from the consequence of excess work.
lessons.body:
## Deep dive 3: Failure and degradation

For ordinary availability-first quotas, limiter failure should not take the whole API down. Security-sensitive checks can require a stricter fallback.

- **Fail open.** If Redis times out (set an aggressive timeout like 5–10 ms), allow the request and emit a metric. Briefly over-admitting is better than rejecting all traffic.
- **Fail closed** only for limits that protect something critical, such as login attempts (brute-force protection) or expensive operations.
- **Local fallback.** Each gateway keeps an approximate in-memory bucket per key, with an explicitly accounted share. When Redis is unreachable, use that instead of nothing.

Dividing an allowance into fixed gateway shares bounds the total only when membership, ownership and resets preserve those shares. Uneven routing can strand allowance on idle gateways, and switching from central state to fresh local buckets can grant extra work unless the transition is accounted for.

## Deep dive 4: Scaling the hot path

At a million checks a second, even one Redis round trip per request adds up. Options:

- **Local pre-check.** Gateways cache "this key is over limit until a given deadline" after a rejection, so a client hammering you is rejected locally without touching Redis.
- **Batching / token leasing.** A gateway takes, say, 10 tokens at a time from Redis and spends them locally. Fully spending each batch can reduce central calls roughly tenfold, but unused reservations can reject requests elsewhere without exceeding the quota. Only lease for keys whose limit is much larger than the total that could be leased out at once : with 200 gateways leasing 10 each, a 100/min customer's whole allowance would be stranded on 10 gateways while requests on the other 190 are rejected.
- **Hot keys.** One huge customer can concentrate load on one Redis shard. Splitting the key into sub-buckets (`key#0..key#7`, each with 1/8 of the limit, picked at random) spreads it. The cost is accuracy: a request can be rejected by an empty sub-bucket while others still have tokens, so this only suits customers whose traffic is large enough to average out.

A small quota may be entirely reserved by a few gateways while requests arriving elsewhere are rejected. Leases must subtract from the central allowance atomically and must not be reclaimed while an old holder could still spend them. Smaller leases or direct checks reduce stranded capacity.

## Deep dive 5: Multiple regions

Should a global limit of 1,000/min be enforced across US and EU together? Assume a cross-region round trip of about 100 ms in this scenario. Putting that round trip on each check would exceed the stated 1–2 ms overhead target. Actual network latency depends on deployment. Options:

- **Per-region limits**: give each region a share (e.g. proportional to its traffic). Simple, slightly unfair if traffic shifts.
- **Async sync**: each region enforces locally and gossips counts to the others every second or so. The global limit can be exceeded by roughly the traffic other regions admit during one sync interval. The amount depends on admission rates, burst allowances and delay; during a partition the delay can grow without bound unless local admission is capped or stopped.

Static regional shares can preserve a global quota if their allowances sum to the limit and redistribution cannot double-allocate. Asynchronous full-quota replicas instead need explicit overshoot and partition bounds.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Tickets at the wrong desk
> Several desks reserve batches from one shared supply. One desk can run out while another still holds unused tickets.
>
> **How it maps:** Token leases reduce trips to shared state but can strand a small allowance away from arriving requests.
>
> **Where it stops:** A network failure cannot safely prove that an old desk stopped spending; lease expiry and reassignment need explicit accounting.

## Key takeaways

- Choose fail-open or fail-closed from the consequence of excess work.
- Lease only when allowance is large enough to avoid stranding small quotas.
- Regional shares and asynchronously replicated full quotas have different overshoot guarantees.

## Further reading

- [Stripe: rate and concurrency limiting](https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters)
- [Cloudflare: measured sliding-counter approximation](https://blog.cloudflare.com/counting-things-a-lot-of-different-things/)

questions.prompt: The Redis cluster backing your limiter has a partial outage: 30% of checks time out. Assume ordinary API quota overruns are acceptable during this outage, while authentication abuse must remain bounded. Which responses fit that policy? Select all that apply.

options.text: Fail open for ordinary API limits: allow the request after a short timeout (~5–10 ms) and emit a metric.
options.explanation: Correct. The limiter exists to protect the API; rejecting 30% of legitimate traffic because the limiter is sick turns a partial limiter outage into an API outage.

options.text: Fail closed for login attempts and password resets.
options.explanation: Correct. These limits defend against brute-force attacks. Briefly rejecting some logins is less harmful than letting attackers try unlimited passwords while the limiter is down.

options.text: Use local buckets with explicitly reserved gateway shares and accounted transitions and resets.
options.explanation: Correct. Fixed shares can bound total allowance only while ownership, membership and reset rules preserve those reservations. Uneven routing can strand allowance.

options.text: Retry each timed-out Redis call up to 5 times before deciding.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Retries multiply load on an already struggling cluster and add tens of milliseconds to every request. Use short timeouts and a fallback, not aggressive retries.

options.text: Return 429 to every request until Redis recovers.
options.explanation: Incorrect. This blocks all customers, including well-behaved ones, making the limiter the cause of a total outage.

questions.workedExample:
Ask, for each limit: **what's worse, over-admitting or rejecting?**

| Limit | Worse outcome | Policy |
|---|---|---|
| API quota | Rejecting paying users | Fail open |
| Login attempts | Brute force | Fail closed |

Then layer a degraded mode: local buckets give protection without a network call only within their accounted allocation and reset policy. Avoid retry storms: a 5 ms timeout with zero retries targets a bounded network wait; scheduling, queueing and the fallback also contribute to measured tail latency while Redis recovers.

questions.prompt: A customer has a global limit of **10,000 requests/minute**, and you serve them from **US and EU** regions. A cross-region round trip is ~90 ms. Which design best balances accuracy and latency?

options.text: Each region enforces locally against a share of the limit; reserve shares so their sum stays within the quota and rebalance without double allocation.
options.explanation: Correct. Local enforcement avoids the 90 ms remote round trip. Static shares can preserve the total allowance but strand capacity in an idle region. Async full-quota replicas require separately justified overshoot bounds.

options.text: Every check in either region goes to a single US Redis cluster.
options.explanation: Wrong. EU requests would pay ~90 ms extra on every call, far over the 1–2 ms budget, and an Atlantic link problem would break EU rate limiting entirely.

options.text: Use a synchronously replicated multi-region database with strong consistency for counters.
options.explanation: Wrong. A commit quorum spanning these regions requires cross-region coordination; the supplied 90 ms round trip would exceed this check's budget. Quorum placement and the client's region determine which requests pay that delay. Strong consistency is overkill for a counter where a few percent overshoot is acceptable.

options.text: Give each region the full 10,000/min limit independently.
options.explanation: Wrong. The customer could get up to 20,000/min, a 100% overshoot. That's a pricing and protection failure, not an acceptable approximation.

questions.workedExample: Reserve disjoint regional shares whose combined allowances stay within the global limit. Each region can then decide locally, but spare quota may remain in a quiet region. Rebalancing must transfer ownership without permitting both regions to spend the same allowance. Giving every region the full quota and exchanging counts later is a different contract: delayed communication and partitions can cause substantial overshoot.

questions.prompt: To save Redis calls, each of **200 gateways** leases **10 tokens** at a time from a client's central bucket. A small customer has **100 tokens available in the current window**, with no refill during this burst and no outstanding earlier leases. Their traffic is spread evenly across all gateways. What goes wrong?

options.text: Nothing: leasing is always accurate because tokens are only spent once.
options.explanation: Wrong. Tokens are spent once, but where they sit matters. Leased tokens are stranded on whichever gateways took them.

options.text: The customer gets 2,000 requests/minute because each gateway gets its own 10.
options.explanation: Wrong. Leases come out of the central bucket, so only 100 tokens are available in this stated window. The problem is the opposite: under-admission.

options.text: The first 10 gateways to ask take all 100 tokens; requests landing on the other 190 gateways are rejected even though most leased tokens sit unused.
options.explanation: Correct. Leasing only works when the limit is large compared with the lease size times the number of gateways. Here 10 × 200 = 2,000 tokens would be needed to give every gateway one lease; the customer has 100.

options.text: Redis load increases, because leasing adds a call per request.
options.explanation: Wrong. Leasing reduces Redis calls; that's its purpose. The issue is accuracy for small limits.

questions.workedExample: The central bucket still limits how many tokens exist. The problem is where they are held: gateways that reserved batches may be idle while other gateways have requests but no allowance. Use direct checks for small quotas, reduce lease sizes, or route work to its reserved capacity. Never reissue unused-looking leased tokens without a protocol that stops the old holder spending them.

lessons.title: Protect in-flight work and total fleet capacity
lessons.summary: Per-client rates cannot bound all fleet traffic or long-running work.
lessons.body:
Earlier units bound request counts for each client. A service can still overload when many compliant clients arrive together, or when a few allowed requests run for a long time. This unit separates admission rate from resource occupancy.

## Bottlenecks and trade-offs

| Choice | Trade-off |
|---|---|
| Central Redis | Shared atomic decisions; network and failover costs |
| Local only | Fast; global accuracy needs reserved shares |
| Fail open | Preserves admission; can allow excess work |
| Fail closed | Bounds admission; can reject legitimate work |

Also mention that rate limiting is not load shedding. Stripe, for example, runs request-rate and concurrency limiters per user *and* fleet-wide load shedding mechanisms that drop low-priority traffic when the whole system is under strain. Per-key limits don't protect you when a million well-behaved clients all arrive at once.

Rate is also not the same as work in progress. Little's law, a general result for any stable queueing system, links them:

```formula reference
L = λW
where
L: mean number of requests in the chosen system, including waiting if it is within that boundary
λ: long-run accepted arrival rate, in requests per second
W: mean time each request spends inside the same boundary, in seconds
In words: in a stable system, average work present grows with both the arrival rate and the time each request stays; a rate cap alone is not an instantaneous concurrency cap.
```

So a customer averaging 100 accepted requests per minute, each spending 20 seconds in the measured system, has about 33 requests present on average, even though the rate limit is respected. Little's law holds only for long-run averages in a stable system (one that keeps up with its arrivals). A **concurrency limiter** (a cap on in-flight requests per customer, say 10) bounds that directly.

## At 10x scale

At 10 million checks/s:

- A central Redis call per request may become expensive; shard count follows a representative script benchmark. Move to **two-tier limiting**: gateways enforce locally with durably reserved token batches. Choose replenishment frequency from measured demand; a periodic count sync alone is not equivalent to safe leasing.
- Push coarse limits (per-IP DDoS protection) to the **edge/CDN** so abusive traffic never reaches your data centre.
- Use **per-region** limits, with periodic rebalancing of each region's share.
- Treat rule changes as a deployment: version them, roll them out gradually, and have a kill switch, because a wrong rule can reject all traffic instantly.

## Key takeaways

- Per-client rates cannot bound all fleet traffic or long-running work.
- Little’s law relates stable long-run averages, not instantaneous concurrency.
- Use concurrency caps, load shedding and gradual rule deployments.

## Further reading

- [Stripe: rate and concurrency limiting](https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters)
- [MIT: Little’s law](https://web.mit.edu/1.041/www/lectures/L3-cumulative-diagram-2026sp.pdf)

questions.prompt: Every customer is within their 100 requests/minute limit, yet the API falls over. A heavy report endpoint takes ~20 s per call, and a sales event has tripled overall traffic. Which mechanisms directly bound concurrent work or shed aggregate overload? Select all that apply.

options.text: A per-customer **concurrency limiter** (for example, at most 5 in-flight report requests).
options.explanation: Correct. Request-rate limits don't cap how much work is in progress. At 100/min with 20 s each, one customer can hold ~33 requests in flight; a concurrency cap bounds that directly.

options.text: A fleet-wide **load shedding** mechanism that drops low-priority traffic when total utilisation is too high.
options.explanation: Correct. Per-key limits can't protect you when every client is individually well-behaved but the total exceeds capacity. Stripe runs fleet-level load shedding mechanisms for exactly this.

options.text: Lower every customer's per-minute limit by half.
options.explanation: Incorrect. It punishes all customers permanently for a temporary capacity problem, and still doesn't bound slow, concurrent work.

options.text: Move the rate limiter from the gateway into each backend service.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Moving the limiter doesn't change what it measures. The gap is concurrency and overall capacity, not limiter placement.

options.text: Prioritise critical traffic (e.g. payments) over less critical (e.g. reports) when shedding.
options.explanation: Correct. Shedding by priority keeps the most important requests flowing while the system is overloaded.

questions.workedExample: A slow report holds resources long after it was admitted. Many such requests can overlap even when the client respects a per-minute limit. Add a concurrency cap for that work and fleet-wide shedding for aggregate overload; use priorities to protect critical requests. Little’s law relates stable averages and does not itself enforce any instantaneous bound.

lessons.title: Size suggestion traffic and snapshot memory
lessons.summary: Debouncing changes the number of requests per search.
lessons.body:
Type "how to" into a search box and suggestions appear before you finish the word. Typing can generate several suggestion requests per search; debouncing and local reuse determine how many actually reach the server.

The trick to this problem is realising that **the serving path should do almost no work**. Precompute expensive counting and candidate selection so the online path starts with a lookup. Current removal rules, trending merges and any personal re-ranking still require bounded serve-time work.

## Step 1: Requirements

**Functional**

- Given a prefix, return the top **k** (say 10) completions.
- Rank by popularity, with some weight for recency so trending queries appear.
- Support multiple languages/locales.
- Never suggest offensive, dangerous or private content.

**Non-functional**

- **Latency**: assume a character every 100–200 ms for this interaction budget. Suggestions should render within ~100 ms end to end, so the server budget is ~10–20 ms.
- **Availability**: if autocomplete is down, search still works, so it's important but not critical. Degrade gracefully (show nothing) rather than slow the search box.
- **Freshness**: a new trending query (breaking news) should appear within minutes to an hour; general popularity can update daily.
- **Eventual consistency** is fine: two users seeing slightly different suggestions is harmless.

Out of scope: spelling correction, full search results.

## Step 2: Estimates

Assume **1 billion searches/day**. Users type ~20 characters per query, but clients **debounce** (wait ~100 ms of idle before sending) and stop once they pick a suggestion, so call it **~6 suggestion requests per search**.

Requests per second are searches per day times requests per search, divided by the seconds in a day:

Measure suggestion requests per completed search: typing pauses, cancellation, cache reuse and selection all affect it. A daily search count does not establish a universal keystroke multiplier or a peak profile.

What to store? Most queries are rare; the long tail is huge and mostly useless for suggestions. Keep the **top ~100 million queries** by frequency.

Size the three parts of the index: the query strings, the trie nodes (one per distinct prefix), and a top-10 list at every node:

The index holds query strings, prefix structure and stored candidate lists. Repeating a top-ten list at many prefix nodes can dominate raw text size; pointer, allocator and child-map overhead depend on representation.

The number of distinct prefixes depends on the actual corpus and maximum prefix depth. Do not infer it from the number of queries alone:

Choose an identifier width that covers every retained query, including reserved values. Compact IDs reduce repeated list payload; they do not account for the rest of the index.

If the measured index and its rollout overlap fit the selected machine’s memory budget, full replication is an option. Measure the built representation: pointers, child maps, strings and allocator overhead can make a naive trie much larger. We'll replicate it rather than shard it, which keeps serving simple. Budget for **two copies** in memory, because a node loads the new trie snapshot before releasing the old one: a 50 GB index wants a machine with well over 100 GB of RAM.

## Key takeaways

- Debouncing changes the number of requests per search.
- Measure the built index; a query count does not prove its memory footprint.
- Budget for old and new snapshots to coexist while readers finish.

## Further reading

- [Finite-state transducers and compact indexes](https://burntsushi.net/transducers/)
- [Elasticsearch: completion suggesters](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/rest-apis/search-suggesters)

options.text: Nothing, because cancellation guarantees the server did no work.

lessons.title: Precompute prefix answers and control client requests
lessons.summary: A top-k list at each prefix removes subtree search from serving.
lessons.body:
## Step 3: API

```
GET /v1/suggest?q=how%20to%20m
              &locale=en-GB&limit=10
-> 200
{ "prefix": "how to m",
  "suggestions": [
    "how to make pancakes",
    "how to meditate", ...] }
Cache-Control: public, max-age=300
```

Client behaviour matters as much as the server:

- **Debounce** keystrokes (~100 ms) so fast typists don't send a request per character.
- **Cancel** in-flight requests when a newer prefix is typed, and ignore stale responses that arrive out of order.
- **Cache locally**: if the user deletes a character, the previous prefix's results are already in memory.
- **Filter locally**: if the suggestions for "how to m" are known, the client can filter them for "how to ma" as provisional results, but that subset may omit the true top completions for the longer prefix; fetch again when complete results matter.

## Step 4: Data model

### The trie

A [trie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trie) stores strings by their characters, one level per character, so all strings sharing a prefix share a path.

```
        (root)
        /    \
       h      t
       |      |
       o      r
      / \     |
     w   t    e
     |   |    |
    ...  e    e
         |
         l
```

A naive lookup walks to the prefix node, one step per character, then searches the entire subtree for the most popular completions. For a short prefix like "s", that subtree contains millions of queries, which is far too slow.

### Precompute top-k at every node

Store the top-k completions **at each node**. Lookup becomes "walk to the node, return its list". The change moves ranking work out of each request:

With a stored candidate list, lookup follows the prefix and reads the selected results instead of searching the entire subtree. The trade-off is extra memory and work when rebuilding the lists.

The response still costs time to copy and transmit its strings.

```
node "how t" -> [how to tie a tie (98k),
                 how to train your dragon,
                 ...]
```

The cost is memory (k entries per node) and rebuild work, but we do that offline. Use compact IDs instead of full strings in each list, and cap prefix depth (beyond ~20–30 characters, there's little to suggest).

### Alternatives

- **Flattened trie in a KV store**: store `prefix → top-k list` directly in Redis or Cassandra. Easy to shard and update; memory relative to a trie depends on key duplication and representation. Good if the index outgrows one machine.
- **Finite-state transducers**: Lucene and Elasticsearch's completion suggester use compact finite-state representations. Equivalent suffix paths can be shared as well as common prefixes; size savings depend on the indexed data and representation.
- **Radix trees** collapse chains of single-child nodes into one edge, saving memory for long unique tails.

## Step 5: High-level design

```
 Browser/app (debounce, cache)
        |
        v
 CDN edge cache
        |  (miss)
        v
 Suggest service x N
 (whole trie in RAM)
        ^
        | load snapshot
 Object store (trie files)
        ^
        | build
 Trie builder (batch)
        ^
        | query counts
 Aggregator (stream + batch)
        ^
        |
 Search logs -> Kafka
```

Two separate paths:

- **Serving path** (top half): read-only, in memory, cached at the edge.
- **Data path** (bottom half): logs → counts → ranked lists → a new trie snapshot every hour or day.

They meet only at the snapshot. The suggest service never writes anything.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: An index with recommendations already attached
> A library’s subject index can include a short recommended-reading list, so a visitor need not inspect every book on that subject.
>
> **How it maps:** The prefix path locates a precomputed candidate list; expensive selection happens when building the index.
>
> **Where it stops:** The list can become stale or omit newly relevant items; personalisation and urgent removal require additional mechanisms.

## Key takeaways

- A top-k list at each prefix removes subtree search from serving.
- Debounce, cancel, ignore stale responses and reuse local results.
- Keep the serving path separate from the snapshot-building pipeline.

## Further reading

- [Meta: the life of a typeahead query](https://engineering.fb.com/2010/05/17/web/the-life-of-a-typeahead-query/)
- [Elasticsearch: completion suggesters](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/rest-apis/search-suggesters)
- [Trie data structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trie)

questions.prompt: In a plain trie (no precomputation), why is finding the top 10 completions for the prefix `s` slow?

options.text: Walking from the root to the node for `s` takes time proportional to the number of stored queries.
options.explanation: Wrong. Reaching the prefix node takes one step per character of the prefix, here a single step. The walk is cheap; what follows isn't.

options.text: Tries can't store popularity scores, so you must query a database for each candidate.
options.explanation: Wrong. Nodes can store any payload, including a score on terminal nodes or a precomputed top-k list. The slowness comes from the traversal, not from missing data.

options.text: The lookup must traverse the whole subtree under `s`, potentially millions of queries, to find the 10 most popular.
options.explanation: Correct. Every query starting with `s` lives below that node. Without precomputed results you have to visit them all (or a large part) and pick the top 10, which is far too slow for a 10–20 ms budget.

options.text: Single-character prefixes cause hash collisions in the trie.
options.explanation: Wrong. Tries aren't hash tables; each character selects a child edge. There's no collision concept here.

questions.workedExample: Reaching the prefix node is cheap because it follows the typed characters. Discovering and ranking completions below that node is the expensive second step. Store a precomputed candidate list at the prefix so serving reads that list instead of traversing the subtree. This shifts work and memory into index construction; response bytes still have a cost.

questions.prompt: Which client-side behaviours reduce load or improve perceived latency for typeahead? Select all that apply.

options.text: Debounce keystrokes, sending a request only after ~100 ms of no typing.
options.explanation: Correct when gaps are shorter than the debounce interval; savings depend on typing cadence.

options.text: Cache responses by prefix in memory so backspacing reuses earlier results.
options.explanation: Correct when the earlier prefix was fetched and its result remains valid; debounce may have skipped it.

options.text: Ignore responses for prefixes older than the current input.
options.explanation: Correct. Responses can arrive out of order; rendering a stale one makes suggestions flicker to an older prefix. Dropping them (or cancelling the request) keeps the UI correct.

options.text: Retry an obsolete prefix three times even after the input has changed.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Obsolete requests should be cancelled or ignored. A still-current prefix can have a small deadline-aware retry policy.

options.text: Send a request for every keystroke so suggestions are always current.
options.explanation: Incorrect. This multiplies load for almost no benefit, since intermediate prefixes are usually never seen by the user.

questions.workedExample: Debounce coalesces short gaps, a valid local cache reuses fetched prefixes, and a prefix or request version prevents stale responses from replacing current suggestions. Neither debounce savings nor cache hits are guaranteed. Retry only still-useful work inside the interaction deadline.

lessons.title: Build fresh suggestions without exposing rare queries
lessons.summary: Rank submitted searches with explicit decay and eligibility rules.
lessons.body:
## Deep dive 1: The data collection pipeline

1. **Log** every submitted search (not every keystroke; we rank on what people *searched*) with timestamp, locale and a pseudonymous user ID (which is not automatically anonymous). At 1B/day, sampling 1 in 10 still gives plenty of signal for popular queries.
2. **Aggregate** with a stream processor (Flink, Kafka Streams) into counts per `(query, locale, hour)`. For truly huge streams, approximate structures such as a [count-min sketch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count%E2%80%93min_sketch) with a heavy-hitters heap find frequent queries in fixed memory.
3. **Score** with time decay so last week counts more than last year (formula below).
4. **Filter**: remove queries on a blocklist (hate, violence, adult), and apply a **privacy threshold**: only consider queries searched by at least a minimum number of distinct users. This reduces rare-query exposure but does not guarantee privacy: sensitive information can be searched by many people or bots. Add explicit sensitive-data filtering and review.
5. **Build** the trie with top-k at every node (Spark job: for every query, emit `(prefix, query, score)` for each of its prefixes, group by prefix, keep the top k). With 100M queries and up to 20 prefixes each, that's up to 2 billion records to shuffle, a substantial batch workload whose duration depends on cluster resources.
6. **Publish** the serialised trie to object storage with a version number. Serving nodes download it, load it into memory alongside the current one, then publish the new root atomically with suitable synchronization. Retain the old trie snapshot until all readers using it finish. Roll out to a few nodes first and compare metrics, just like a code deploy.

The time-decayed score in step 3 weights each day's searches by how old they are:

```formula reference
S = Σ(c_d a^{t_d})
where
S: ranking score from the retained daily search counts
Σ: sum over all retained days d
d: a day whose search count contributes to the score
c_d: eligible search count on day d
a: daily retention factor, greater than zero and less than one
t_d: age of day d in days, with zero for today
In words: older searches count less, with each extra day multiplying their weight by the same factor; a smaller factor favours recent activity more strongly.
```

The decay factor sets the trade-off: closer to 1 (say 0.98) keeps long-term favourites; smaller (say 0.7) makes suggestions chase the last few days.

### Freshness for trending queries

A daily rebuild can't surface "earthquake in Tokyo" ten minutes after it happens. Add a small **trending overlay**: the stream aggregator tracks queries whose last-hour count is far above their baseline, and the suggest service merges this small "trending" list into results for matching prefixes. The big trie stays daily; only a few thousand trending entries change minute to minute.

### Removing a suggestion urgently

Sometimes a suggestion must disappear *now*: a defamatory phrase, a victim's name, a legal takedown. Waiting for tomorrow's build isn't acceptable, and the CDN may hold the bad response for its whole TTL. So:

- Keep a small **serve-time blocklist** that every suggest node checks before returning results. It's pushed in seconds, like a config change.
- **Purge** affected prefixes using the selected CDN's documented purge mechanism, or keep edge TTLs short enough that the worst-case exposure is acceptable.
- Add the term to the pipeline's blocklist so the next build drops it at source.

A distinct-user threshold does not prevent campaigns using many accounts. Cap repeated contributions per identity and review concentrated growth across accounts or network sources. Uniform log sampling reduces both bot and human counts in expectation; it does not selectively remove manipulation.

## Key takeaways

- Rank submitted searches with explicit decay and eligibility rules.
- A distinct-user threshold reduces rare exposure but is not a privacy guarantee.
- Combine a trending overlay, serve-time blocklist and cache purge for urgent changes.

## Further reading

- [Meta: the life of a typeahead query](https://engineering.fb.com/2010/05/17/web/the-life-of-a-typeahead-query/)
- [Exponential decay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_decay)

questions.prompt: Your trie rebuilds once a day. Product wants breaking-news queries (e.g. a major earthquake) to appear in suggestions **within 10 minutes**. What's the most practical design?

options.text: Add a small trending overlay: a stream job detects queries spiking above their baseline and publishes a small trending list that the suggest service merges into results.
options.explanation: Correct. Bound the trending layer to an explicit candidate budget and index by prefix. The main trie remains a daily artifact; measure merge latency and enforce the same safety/privacy filtering on both paths.

options.text: Update trie nodes in place on the serving nodes on every search.
options.explanation: Wrong. Updating top-k lists along every prefix path on every search means ~20 writes per search at 1B+ searches a day, with locking on hot nodes like 's'. It destroys the read-only simplicity that makes serving fast.

options.text: Rebuild the full trie every 10 minutes.
options.explanation: Wrong. A full rebuild aggregates weeks of logs and processes hundreds of millions of queries; meeting a ten-minute rebuild cadence requires resources and measured completion time that this design has not established, and each rebuild plus rollout might not even finish in 10 minutes.

options.text: Lower the CDN TTL to zero.
options.explanation: Wrong. Edge caching isn't the bottleneck; even with no caching, the underlying trie wouldn't contain the new query until the next daily build.

questions.workedExample: Keep the large stable index on its normal rebuild cadence. A stream pipeline compares recent activity with an explicit baseline and publishes a bounded, prefix-indexed trending overlay. Apply the same abuse, privacy and removal rules to both sources before merging. Measure merge latency and rollout delay; a small overlay does not guarantee either is negligible.

questions.prompt: A privacy review finds that a user's unusual search, including their full home address, appeared as a suggestion for others. Which pipeline change reduces this class of exposure while acknowledging that popularity alone cannot prove privacy?

options.text: Add the user's address to the blocklist.
options.explanation: Wrong as a fix. It removes this one case but not the class of problem; every other user's private query can still leak. Blocklists are for known bad terms, not for unpredictable personal data.

options.text: Encrypt the search logs at rest.
options.explanation: Wrong. Encryption protects logs from unauthorised access, but the pipeline still decrypts and counts them. The query would still become a suggestion.

options.text: Shorten the CDN TTL so the suggestion disappears faster.
options.explanation: Wrong. This only changes how long cached copies live; the next trie build would still include the query.

options.text: Require a distinct-user eligibility threshold plus sensitive-data filtering and review; do not treat the threshold as a privacy guarantee.
options.explanation: Correct. A threshold suppresses rare queries, but addresses and other personal information can be searched by many people or attacker accounts. Approximate distinct counts can also overestimate; validate eligibility conservatively.

questions.workedExample:
Find where private data enters the suggestions: the aggregator counts raw searches, and a single user searching the same thing repeatedly can push it high enough for a narrow prefix.

Fix it at aggregation:

This Python fixture implements the distinct-identity threshold for one locale. Its input identities are assumed eligible; bot detection and sensitive-data filtering remain separate requirements.

```python
# Fixture: repeated events from one user
# still count as only one identity.
events = {
    "rare": ["u1"] * 100,
    "popular": [
        f"u{i}" for i in range(50)
    ],
}
keep = []
for query, users in events.items():
    # Count each eligible identity once.
    distinct_users = len(set(users))
    if distinct_users < 50:
        continue
    keep.append(query)
print(keep)
# ['popular']: rare has only one user.
```

A HyperLogLog can estimate candidate popularity, but its probabilistic estimate alone cannot prove that a strict eligibility threshold was reached. Counting distinct users also resists manipulation, since a bot repeating a phrase from one account gains nothing. Then add a blocklist and PII detectors (addresses, phone numbers) as additional risk reduction, with explicit review and removal procedures; none of these alone guarantees privacy.

questions.prompt: A ranking system multiplies every existing contribution by the same daily decay factor. Queries A and B receive no new searches. If A currently scores above B, what happens solely because another day passes?

options.text: B automatically overtakes A because it was originally searched more recently.
options.explanation: Both existing scores receive the same new factor, so recency alone does not reverse their current order.

options.text: Both scores shrink by the same proportion, so their relative order stays the same.
options.explanation: Correct under the stated common factor and no new activity; new contributions or another ranking rule can change it.

options.text: A stays unchanged until a fixed thirty-day expiry.
options.explanation: Exponential decay applies continuously by the chosen time step; it is not a hard expiry rule.

options.text: The higher score always loses more proportionally until they tie.
options.explanation: The absolute loss is larger, but the proportional change is the same.

questions.workedExample: Each contribution becomes one day older, so the same daily multiplier applies to every contribution and therefore to both totals. A different factor changes how strongly the system favours new activity, but elapsed time alone does not make one unchanged history overtake another under the same factor.

questions.prompt: Legal asks you to remove a defamatory suggestion **immediately**. Suggestions are cached at the CDN for 10 minutes and the trie rebuilds nightly. Which steps belong in your answer? Select all that apply.

options.text: Push the phrase to a serve-time blocklist that every suggest node checks before responding.
options.explanation: Correct. A small blocklist distributed like config takes effect in seconds on the origin, without waiting for a rebuild.

options.text: Purge the affected prefixes from the CDN.
options.explanation: Correct. Otherwise the edge keeps serving the cached response for up to 10 minutes after the origin is fixed.

options.text: Add the phrase to the pipeline's blocklist so tonight's build drops it at source.
options.explanation: Correct. The serve-time list is a stopgap; fixing the source stops it reappearing in the next snapshot.

options.text: Trigger an immediate full rebuild and wait for it to roll out.
options.explanation: Incorrect as the main action. No rebuild duration is established here, and rebuilding still leaves existing CDN copies stale. It's far slower than the blocklist plus purge.

options.text: Set the CDN TTL to zero permanently.
options.explanation: Incorrect. It sacrifices most of your offload to handle a rare event that purging handles well.

questions.workedExample:
Trace every layer where the bad suggestion lives:

| Layer | Lifetime | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Trie snapshot | until rebuild | pipeline blocklist |
| Suggest node | until rebuild | serve-time blocklist |
| CDN | 10 min | purge |
| Browser | its cache TTL | accept, or keep short |

A strong answer names each layer and the fastest lever for it.

questions.prompt: Bots search "cheap pills brand-x" 500,000 times in a day from 300 accounts so it becomes a top suggestion for "cheap". Your pipeline already has a 50-distinct-user threshold. What's the best additional defence?

options.text: Rank by distinct users (or cap each user's contribution), and flag queries whose growth is concentrated in a few accounts or IPs.
options.explanation: Correct. 300 accounts doing 500k searches is ~1,700 each, nothing like organic behaviour. Counting each user at most a few times strips most of the inflated count, and concentration anomalies flag the campaign.

options.text: Raise the distinct-user threshold to 1,000.
options.explanation: Partly helps, but attackers can create more accounts, and a high threshold hides genuine niche queries for smaller locales. It's a blunt tool on its own.

options.text: Sample logs 1 in 100 so the bot's searches mostly get dropped.
options.explanation: Wrong. Uniform independent sampling reduces bot and human counts in the same proportion in expectation. Random variation can change ranks, but it does not selectively remove the manipulation.

options.text: Turn off suggestions for the prefix "cheap".
options.explanation: Wrong. It removes a useful prefix for everyone and the bots simply move to another prefix.

questions.workedExample: A distinct-user threshold alone can be passed by many attacker-controlled accounts. Cap repeated contributions per identity and examine concentration and unusual growth, while recognising that identities and IPs are imperfect signals. Uniform sampling reduces human and bot counts alike in expectation. Combine these signals with review and removal; no single threshold proves a query is safe or organic.
